input:
With the corrosion allowance duly taken into account, the compressor wall thickness comes to 86 mm, the allowance, rather than the pressure duty itself, accounting for the difference from the thickness a purely pressure-based calculation would require. The corrosion allowance is extra metal deliberately added beyond the thickness required to withstand the pressure, so that the wall still carries the pressure duty after the anticipated loss of metal over the design life. The specified thickness therefore already embodies its own built-in margin for wastage, and any future measurement that comes in below 86 mm reads against this known starting point rather than against the bare pressure minimum.

The comparison between the two candidate gasket materials has been structured around one criterion only, namely the temperature limit. Other factors, such as pressure rating, seating behaviour and cost, have not been brought into the comparison, since it was set up on the temperature limit and its scope should not expand retrospectively. Of the two materials, one offers the higher temperature limit, and the preference falls on the higher-rated material for those joints whose temperatures the compressor may approach in service. A gasket whose limit the duty can reach leaves no margin for the excursions that accompany start-up and load change, and providing that margin is the entire purpose of the comparison.

Set against this preference is the profile of the duty itself. The time actually spent near the temperature limit is the quantity that determines how much margin the joint genuinely requires, and the duty record assembled so far covers steady running considerably more thoroughly than transients, meaning that the weight placed on the higher limit rests largely on the part of the duty that is least completely documented, and the argument remains open on that ground

Corrosion allowance is metal added beyond the thickness the pressure calculation requires, so that the wall still carries the pressure duty after the expected metal loss over the design life. The specified thickness therefore contains its own wastage margin, and a later measurement below 86 mm reads against a known starting value rather than against the pressure minimum alone.

The gasket choice at the compressor flanges turns on temperature limit alone. Pressure rating, seating behaviour and price are not compared, because the comparison was set up on the temperature limit and the record of the comparison does not widen after the fact. Of the two materials, one carries the higher temperature limit, and the preference follows that limit: the higher-rated material is preferred for the joints whose temperature the compressor can approach in service. A gasket whose limit the duty can reach leaves no margin for the excursions that accompany start-up and load change, and the margin is the point of the comparison.

Against the preference stands the duty profile itself. Time spent near the temperature limit is the quantity that decides how much margin the joint needs, and the duty record assembled so far covers steady running better than it covers transients, so the weight placed on the higher limit rests on the part of the duty that is least completely recorded, and the hours near the limit stay uncounted in the argument as it stands
